item.title: Cyborg bacteria as semi-living organelles for the augmentation of mammalian cells.
item.abstract: Synthetic organelles are engineered to replicate the compartmentalization and dynamic functionality of natural organelles, offering the potential to reprogram or rescue cellular functions. Existing approaches, such as protein cages, biomolecular condensates, and other artificial compartments, have shown promise but remain limited by their capacity to perform multifunctional tasks. To overcome these challenges, we introduce Cyborg Bacterial Organelles (CBOs), which are non-replicating, metabolically active bacteria engineered to function as living synthetic organelles within mammalian cells. Unlike synthetic systems or replicating endosymbionts, CBOs integrate the biological complexity of living organisms with the stability and tunability of engineered materials. CBOs are generated by permeating bacteria with poly(ethylene glycol) diacrylate (PEG) based monomers followed by intracellular UV induced hydrogel crosslinking, producing a structurally reinforced, non-replicative chassis capable of sustained activity inside host cells. Here, we show that CBOs remained detectable inside mammalian cells with substantially reduced morphological disruption compared with wild-type bacteria. Furthermore, we show that CBOs can perform complex functions intracellularly, including responses to extracellular chemical stimuli via synthetic gene circuits and execution of enzymatic reactions such as prodrug conversion into a therapeutic drug. Notably, we also show that CBOs protect host cells from chemically induced mitochondrial stress. Transcriptomic analysis revealed host gene expression changes associated with membrane remodeling, ion transport, and metabolic buffering, suggesting that CBOs modulate the host in protective and adaptive ways. Together, these findings establish CBOs as a novel hybrid material platform for intracellular engineering while addressing key limitations of current synthetic organelle systems. CBOs open new possibilities for cellular modulation in therapeutic and diagnostic applications.

item.title: Polaris: A toolkit for standardized construction, integration, and quantitative testing in Escherichia coli and Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
item.abstract: Existing synthetic biology toolkits have expanded part libraries and assembly capabilities. However, new users may still encounter ambiguity in construct definitions, hierarchical transitions, genomic integration routes, and quantitative testing procedures. Here, we present Polaris, a Golden Gate toolkit for Escherichia coli and Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Polaris uses a MoClo-derived three-level hierarchy. Level 1 stores reusable parts, Level 2 generates transcription units and other intermediate constructs, and Level 3 supports multigene assembly and switching between testing and integration backbones. The toolkit distinguishes part interfaces from transcription unit interfaces, uses BpiI and BsaI in successive assembly stages, and provides parallel ccdB and mScarletI3 screening options. Integration modules and quantitative characterization frameworks were implemented in both hosts and demonstrated using representative genetic parts and activation and repression systems. A companion digital platform further encodes the Level 1 to Level 3 rules for assembly planning. Polaris connects hierarchical construction, stable genetic implementation, and quantitative testing within a common execution framework, providing a practical basis for data accumulation, part standardization, and future automation.

item.title: CRISPR-Cas gene regulation in mycobacteria: From single-gene targeting to dynamic network rewiring.
item.abstract: Mycobacteria represent both clinically important pathogens and valuable microbial chassis, creating a demand for precise and scalable gene-regulatory technologies. However, conventional genetic approaches suffer from inefficient recombination, lengthy strain construction, and restricted capacity for multiplex manipulation. The application of diverse CRISPR-Cas systems in mycobacterial genetics has substantially expanded the genetic toolbox available for these organisms, enabling programmable genome editing and transcriptional regulation. Among these platforms, Cas9-based systems have facilitated essential-gene interrogation and resistance-associated genetic screens; however, their broader application is constrained by protospacer adjacent motif (PAM) dependence, DNA-break-associated toxicity, and limited multiplex capability. Cas12-family effectors, characterized by their distinct PAM preferences, compact architectures, and intrinsic CRISPR RNA (crRNA) processing capacity, provide alternative strategies for expanding target accessibility and regulatory scalability. Here, we critically review the development of CRISPR-based regulatory platforms in mycobacteria, focusing on the transition from the Cas9-centered single-gene manipulation toward the Cas12-enabled multiplex and network-level regulation. We discuss emerging miniature effectors and dynamic regulatory modules that may overcome current limitations in target coverage, temporal control, and host compatibility. Finally, we highlight key engineering challenges and future directions toward programmable regulatory systems integrating protein engineering, synthetic biology, and spatiotemporal control, with potential applications in tuberculosis research and mycobacterial metabolic engineering.

item.title: Guide DNAs Program Enzyme for Detection of Circulating Tumor DNA Without Target Denaturation and Amplification.
item.abstract: Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) is fragmented, tumor-derived cell-free double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) whose low abundance and limited sequence accessibility complicate detection under mild conditions. Here we show that guide DNAs (gDNAs) can program an exonuclease to interrogate native dsDNA under mild conditions and convert this access into a single-molecule fluorescence readout. We found that gDNA 5'-terminal chemistry regulates λ exonuclease (λExo) recruitment. Among those termini, anionic 5'-phosphate and 5'-carboxyl-C10 phosphate enabled the strongest target-dependent processing. Molecular simulations suggested a possible structural basis for these activity differences based on terminal positioning within the catalytic pocket. Coupling the optimized 5'-carboxyl-C10 phosphate gDNA with 10-23 DNAzyme turnover generated a single-molecule fluorescence readout without target nucleic-acid amplification. The assay detected dsDNA down to 10 fM across 10-1000 fM, showed a statistically significant response at an epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) L858R mutant fraction of 0.05% under the tested conditions, and was applied to 24 plasma samples (12 from patients with non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and 12 from healthy donors), achieving 91.7% sensitivity, 100% specificity, 95.8% accuracy, and an area under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve (AUC) of 0.97. This work establishes gDNA-programmed enzyme access as a route for detecting low-abundance duplex tumor DNA.

item.title: The Global Landscape of Liquid Biopsy Technology in Oncology: From Biological Foundations to Commercial and Clinical Frontiers.
item.abstract: Liquid biopsy has developed rapidly over the past decade and now contributes to several defined areas of oncology practice. Here, we offer an expert opinion on the biological foundations, technological platforms, clinical evidence base, commercial ecosystem and market trajectory of blood-based cancer diagnostics as of mid-2026. We critically evaluate the four principal circulating analytes, cell-free DNA (cfDNA) and its tumour-shed fraction circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA), circulating tumour cells (CTCs), extracellular vesicles (EVs) and tumour-educated platelets (TEPs), alongside the analytical platforms that extract clinically actionable signals from them, including high-sensitivity next-generation sequencing, digital droplet polymerase chain reaction, enzymatic and immunoprecipitation-based methylome profiling, genome-wide fragmentomics, long-read sequencing platforms and the increasingly central role of artificial intelligence in multi-omic signal integration. The principal prospective trials are appraised with attention to both their findings and their limitations, including DYNAMIC, TRACERx, IMvigor011, PATHFINDER 2, the National Health Service (NHS)-Galleri and ECLIPSE. The full spectrum of Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved companion diagnostics is reviewed in conjunction with the rapidly maturing startup ecosystem, which spans multi-cancer early detection, minimal residual disease monitoring and circulating-tumour-cell-based multi-omics, alongside the consolidating mergers and acquisitions landscape, with explicit reference to announcements made at the 2026 meetings of the American Society of Clinical Oncology and the American Association for Cancer Research. Non-plasma biofluid substrates including cerebrospinal fluid, urine, saliva and pleural fluid are also discussed for tumour-type-specific applications. The global liquid biopsy market, projected to grow from US$6.17 billion in 2024 to approximately US$22.69 billion by 2034, is analysed by technology, application and geography. We argue that, despite the technical progress documented herein, three structural barriers, namely reimbursement fragmentation, clonal-haematopoiesis-driven biological noise and the persistent absence of prospective mortality data for multi-cancer early detection, together with the fundamental biological limits on ctDNA shedding in low-shedding tumour types and in early-stage disease, must be resolved before liquid biopsy can be applied effectively at the population level.

item.title: Toll-Like Receptors in Mycoplasma Infections: Immunopathogenesis, Cheminformatics, and Machine Learning-Based Insights into TLR-Targeted Therapeutics.
item.abstract: Mycoplasma species are the minimal-genome pathogens that elicit complex host immune responses involving both protective and pathogenic inflammation. Toll-like receptors (TLRs) are pivotal components of the immune system, recognizing pathogen-associated molecular patterns and damage-associated molecular patterns to initiate immune responses. TLRs recognize Mycoplasma-derived lipoproteins, glycolipids, and CpG-rich DNA motifs, initiating NF-κB and MAPK signaling cascades. While these pathways are indispensable for microbial clearance, their dysregulation contributes to chronic inflammation, autoimmunity, and tissue damage. Consequently, selective modulation of TLR signaling has emerged as a promising therapeutic strategy for restoring immune homeostasis. In this study, we summarized the recent advances in delineating the molecular crosstalk between TLRs and Mycoplasma, emphasizing the distinct roles of TLRs in pathogen recognition and immunopathology. In parallel, it integrates a cheminformatics-based analysis of TLR inhibitory ligands retrieved from the ChEMBL database, encompassing over 230 compounds across TLR1-5. Multivariate visualization techniques such as principal component analysis (PCA), uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP), and t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE) were employed to map the chemical space and reveal receptor-specific clustering patterns. The analysis identified TLR2 and TLR4 inhibitors as occupying distinct but overlapping chemical regions, characterized by higher molecular weight, lipophilicity, and structural complexity. Correlation and similarity mapping further highlighted scaffold conservation among active ligands, providing a quantitative foundation for rational drug design and structure-activity modeling. Furthermore, we explore how machine learning (ML) and computational modeling are reshaping TLR-targeted drug discovery. ML-driven frameworks facilitate ligand prediction, virtual screening, and structure-activity optimization through deep docking and transformer-based scoring models. Integrative ML approaches also extend beyond ligand discovery to encompass multiomics data integration, biomarker identification, and predictive modeling of host-pathogen interactions and immune responses. By bridging immunological insight with cheminformatics and ML-based analytics, this article outlines a multidisciplinary roadmap for precision immunomodulation in Mycoplasma-associated diseases. The convergence of experimental pharmacology and computational intelligence holds the potential to accelerate the discovery of next-generation TLR-targeted therapeutics, advancing personalized strategies for immune regulation and infection control.

item.title: Mesenchymal stem cell exosome-mediated immune-fibrosis crosstalk: a novel framework for repairing multi-organ fibrosis.
item.abstract: Multi-organ fibrosis is the common endpoint of chronic inflammatory injury across tissues, affecting organs such as the lung, kidney, liver, heart, and skin. It is marked by persistent immune imbalance, myofibroblast activation, excess matrix deposition, and impaired repair, yet no disease-modifying therapy is available. Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) act mainly through paracrine signals rather than direct differentiation, and mesenchymal stem cell-derived exosomes (MSC-Exos) are key vehicles of this secretome. They carry miRNAs, lncRNAs, proteins, and lipids that mediate intercellular communication, and their low immunogenicity and modifiability make them attractive for cell-free therapy. This review examines MSC-Exos in multi-organ fibrosis, focusing on shared and tissue-specific actions. These vesicles shift macrophages away from proinflammatory states, suppress lymphocyte and innate immune activation, and interfere with NF-κB/NLRP3, TGF-β/Smad, and PI3K/Akt/mTOR signaling, thereby breaking the loop that links inflammation to fibrosis. In parallel, they attenuate epithelial-mesenchymal transition in hepatic stellate cells, renal tubular cells, alveolar epithelium, and cardiac fibroblasts through KLF6/STAT3, YAP/LOXL2, and Wnt/β-catenin axes, while limiting collagen deposition, ferroptosis, and pyroptosis and promoting autophagy. The review then compares MSC-Exos from umbilical cord, adipose, bone marrow, and endometrial MSCs in source, cargo, and reported potency, and surveys engineering, preconditioning, and delivery strategies. However, isolation methods remain inconsistent, tissue-specific signals are poorly defined, preclinical dosing often exceeds clinically feasible levels, and long-term safety data are scarce. Engineered MSC-Exos, improved targeting, and biomaterial-based delivery are promising, but evidence for reversing established fibrosis remains limited.

item.title: Molecular Diagnostics-Guided Immunosuppression Minimization to Belatacept Monotherapy in Kidney Transplant Recipients.
item.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Minimally invasive molecular diagnostics, including donor-derived cell-free DNA (dd-cfDNA) and gene expression profiling, reliably distinguish immune quiescence from allograft injury; however, their utility in guiding immunosuppression minimization has not been fully evaluated.
METHODS: We conducted a 12-month prospective, single-arm observational proof of concept study to determine whether integration of dd-cfDNA (AlloSure), gene expression profiling (AlloMap), and conventional clinical biomarkers could facilitate immunosuppression reduction toward belatacept monotherapy in kidney transplant recipients. Adult recipients ≥9 months post-transplant receiving belatacept-based immunosuppression with stable renal function (eGFR >40 mL/min/1.73 m2), AlloSure ≤1%, and no donor-specific antibodies were enrolled. A three-month lead-in period confirmed immune quiescence prior to stepwise immunosuppression reduction.
RESULTS: Of 25 consented participants, 23 completed the lead-in period. Median dd-cfDNA remained <0.2% throughout follow-up, renal function remained stable, and no episodes of biopsy-proven acute rejection or de novo donor-specific antibodies occurred. One for-cause biopsy performed for transient creatinine elevation demonstrated no rejection. Overall, 52% of participants underwent immunosuppression reduction and 17% achieved belatacept monotherapy. Elevated AlloMap scores were the primary barrier to further reduction despite reassuring clinical and dd-cfDNA markers.
CONCLUSION: Molecular diagnostics-guided immunosuppression minimization was safe in carefully selected belatacept-treated kidney transplant recipients, supporting further evaluation of biomarker-guided strategies to individualize long-term immunosuppression.

item.title: Clonal hematopoiesis in solid tumors: mutant hematopoietic cells as a tumor-microenvironment component across source, lineage and treatment.
item.abstract: Clonal hematopoiesis (CH) introduces a hematopoietic component into the molecular and immune landscape of solid tumors. Its interpretation depends on whether a variant is measured in blood, plasma or tumor tissue, which cells carry it, and when sampling occurs relative to treatment. Existing reviews have examined cancer-associated inflammation, therapy-related clonal selection and clinical outcomes; a less developed question is how these observations can be compared when they measure different aspects of the same clone. This focused narrative review connects source attribution with immune-cell state, tissue localization and longitudinal change, separating human associations from cellular localization and experimental perturbation. Paired leukocyte analysis can identify hematopoietic variants that would otherwise be assigned to cancer cells. Mutation-resolved tissue measurements add information about local immune interactions, whereas serial blood measurements help distinguish clonal selection from the relative prominence of CH when tumor-derived plasma DNA declines. Genotype-specific findings, particularly involving TET2 and myeloid function, provide mechanistic explanations for some treatment associations, but aggregate CH has shown inconsistent relationships with immune-checkpoint efficacy and toxicity. The resulting framework links each measurement to its appropriate biological or clinical use: source correction is already actionable, while treatment prediction and organ-specific risk assessment require evidence that CH adds information beyond established tumor and patient characteristics.

item.title: Mesenchymal Stem Cell-Derived Extracellular Vesicles in Acute Kidney Injury: Sourcing, Characteristics, and Prospects for Clinical Application.
item.abstract: Approximately 13.3 million people each year are affected by acute kidney injury (AKI). Current treatments for AKI are mainly supportive, with no established definitive treatment. However, advances in regenerative medicine have made mesenchymal stem cell-derived extracellular vesicles (MSC-EVs) a promising cell-free therapy for AKI. Across preclinical models, MSC-EVs from different tissue origins consistently alleviated AKI, primarily through paracrine signaling and by restoring mitochondrial function. Despite promising preclinical animal data, small-scale, short-term studies constrain MSC-EV translation to human use. Translating MSC-EV-based treatments to clinical settings is still in its infancy, with no regulatory approvals. This review defines, characterizes, and classifies MSC-EVs; describes the bio-cargoes they carry; and examines the mechanisms by which MSC-EVs from different origins confer renoprotection in AKI models. In doing so, we provide novel insight into functional differences not only between MSC-EVs from conventional tissue sources but also between newly emerging sources, which recent literature has not systematically addressed or integrated. To provide a comprehensive narrative, we also summarize several limitations that impede the use of MSC-EVs in preclinical and clinical settings and critically discuss ways to improve their feasibility for therapeutic application.

item.title: M1 macrophage extracellular vesicles alleviate IL-33-driven group 2 innate lymphoid cell-dominant airway inflammation.
item.abstract: Recently, an increasing number of reports have suggested that group 2 innate lymphoid cells (ILC2s) play a critical role in allergic diseases. Previous studies have observed a positive correlation between the number of different types of ILCs and M1 and M2 macrophages in asthma. Extracellular vesicles (EVs) derived from M1 macrophages (M1 EVs) have high biosafety and low immunogenicity, making them promising cell-free therapeutic agents that provide significant advantages in tumor therapy. However, their function in regulating ILC2s responses remains unclear. Therefore, in this study, M1 EVs were produced to investigate their role in IL-33-driven ILC2s-dominant airway inflammation. The morphology, size, and specific markers of the M1 EVs were successfully characterized. We observed that airway administration of low-dose M1 EVs effectively inhibited ILC2s activation, inflammatory cell infiltration, and lung mucus production, and reduced levels of Th2 cytokines. Through qPCR analysis, we found that the long non-coding RNA IGF2BP1-AS may be involved in mediating these effects of M1 EVs. Furthermore, M1 EVs also displayed favorable safety performance. In conclusion, we demonstrated that low dose M1 EVs were able to at least partially block ILC2s-mediated airway inflammation via IGF2BP1-AS, suggesting that M1 EVs may be a novel cell-free means of treating type 2 immunopathologic diseases such as eosinophilic asthma.

item.title: Au-decorated Ag3PO4 heterostructures as ROS-generating platforms for antitumor and antifungal applications.
item.abstract: In this study, an Au-decorated Ag3PO4 heterostructure (Ag3PO4:Au) was synthesized and evaluated regarding its antitumor and antifungal activities, as well as its underlying mechanisms of action. The biological performance was investigated using MB49 bladder cancer cells through viability, clonogenic, migration, and intracellular ROS assays. At a concentration of 0.12 mg mL-1, Ag3PO4 reduced MB49 cell viability to approximately 50%, whereas Ag3PO4:Au decreased viability to only 9%, while maintaining more than 90% viability in non-tumour L929 fibroblasts. The Ag3PO4:Au heterostructure significantly reduced tumour cell viability and impaired clonogenic survival and migratory capacity, reducing colony formation by more than 80% and reducing wound closure after 48 h, which may reflect reduced migration and/or impaired cell viability or proliferation. Both materials induced an intracellular oxidative response in MB49 and L929 cells (DCF-DA). In cell-free photocatalytic experiments under visible-light, the RhB degradation efficiency of Ag3PO4:Au decreased from 94% to 60% and 20% with TBA and BQ, respectively, indicating participation of •OH and •O₂- in the photocatalytic oxidation process. These experiments characterize the ROS-generating capability of the materials and do not identify the species acting inside the cells. FAAS analyses demonstrated limited ionic release after 24 h, corresponding to less than 5% of the total metal content, with Ag3PO4 releasing 4.12 μg mL-1 of Ag+ and Ag3PO4:Au releasing 3.98 μg mL-1 of Ag+ and 0.73 μg mL-1 of Au ions. In addition, the material exhibited pronounced antifungal activity against Candida albicans, reducing the minimum inhibitory concentration from 250 μg mL-1 for Ag3PO4 to 62.5 μg mL-1 for Ag3PO4:Au. Overall, the results demonstrate that Au NPs decoration effectively modulates the surface properties and ROS-related behaviour of Ag3PO4, translating into improved biological performance. This heterostructure represents a promising multifunctional platform for biomedical applications.

item.title: Hypoxia-primed human adipose-derived stem cell secretome accelerates gastric ulcer healing and promotes tissue remodeling in a murine model.
item.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The secretome of adipose-derived stem cells (ADSCs), collected as conditioned medium (CM), has shown potential as a cell-free approach for gastrointestinal mucosal repair. However, standard normoxic culture produces a basal secretome that may be insufficient to achieve high-quality mucosal regeneration in severe lesions. Although microenvironmental preconditioning can enrich the secretome, in vivo evidence comparing how distinct stressors, specifically hypoxia and oxidative stress, differentially influence the structural and molecular features of gastric ulcer healing at a single repair stage remains limited.
OBJECTIVE: To compare the therapeutic efficacy and morphomolecular profiles of concentrated CM derived from human ADSCs cultured under standard normoxia (Nor-CM), hypoxia (Hypo-CM), and sublethal oxidative stress (H2O2-CM) in a murine model of acetic acid-induced chronic gastric ulcer at Day 7 after induction.
METHODS: Following in vitro preconditioning and concentration, the secretomes were administered intragastrically to mice for 6 consecutive days. Repair parameters were evaluated on Day 7 using systemic body weight recovery, macroscopic morphometry, phenotypic histopathology (H&E), functional restitution of the mucosal barrier (PAS), and transcriptional profiling of apoptotic, inflammatory, and pro-regenerative networks. Cohen's d effect sizes with 95% confidence intervals were reported alongside hypothesis testing to quantify the magnitude of biological effects in the context of inherent in vivo variability.
RESULTS: Hypoxic preconditioning enhanced secretome yield and in vivo therapeutic performance. Hypo-CM showed a strong trend toward accelerated systemic weight recovery (11.35 ± 5.70% vs. Sham, 4.45 ± 9.50%; p = 0.195, d = 0.88, 95% CI [-0.04, 1.80]) and produced the highest incidence of complete macroscopic re-epithelialization (3/10, 30%), although the difference in incidence was not significant (p = 0.582 vs. Sham, 1/10). Histologically, healed Hypo-CM specimens uniquely showed restoration of a continuous, surface-localized mucin layer, in contrast to the reactive mucin accumulation within deep glands observed with unprimed treatment. At the molecular level, Hypo-CM was associated with a favorable immunomodulatory and structural profile on Day 7, with attenuation of pro-inflammatory signaling (IL-6, d = 0.43; TNF-α, d = 0.54) and marked downregulation of hepatocyte growth factor (HGF, d = 0.87 vs. Sham). This reduction in HGF expression on Day 7, together with histological re-epithelialization, was consistent with a transition from active cellular proliferation to mucosal remodeling. In contrast, H2O2-CM showed moderate structural efficacy but maintained an altered inflammatory profile, with suppressed TNF-α and elevated IL-6 (d = 0.50), accompanied by persistent cystic glandular dilation. Nor-CM showed the weakest overall efficacy, with tissues remaining in an incompletely repaired, HGF-elevated state.
CONCLUSION: The in vitro preconditioning microenvironment markedly influences the functional efficacy of the ADSC secretome on Day 7 after ulcer induction. Hypoxic preconditioning enhances secretome potency, promotes resolution of acute inflammatory gene expression, and supports structural tissue remodeling and restoration of the mucosal barrier during chronic gastric ulcer repair.

item.title: Exercise-Derived Skeletal Muscle Exosomes Ameliorate Intervertebral Disc Degeneration and Restore Mitochondrial Homeostasis in Nucleus Pulposus Cells.
item.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Intervertebral disc degeneration (IVDD) is a major cause of chronic low back pain and is characterized by oxidative-stress-associated mitochondrial dysfunction and phenotypic imbalance in nucleus pulposus cells (NPCs). Because the nucleus pulposus is avascular, circulating exercise-derived signals may have limited access to the disc. This preclinical study evaluated locally delivered exercise-derived skeletal muscle exosomes (ESMEs) as a cell-free, exercise-mimetic preparation for protecting NPCs and attenuating IVDD.
METHODS: A rat exercise model was established to isolate ESMEs, with non-exercise skeletal muscle exosomes (NSMEs) as controls. In an H2O2-induced oxidative-injury NPC model, apoptosis, senescence, extracellular matrix metabolism, mitochondrial function, ROS, and mitochondrial quality-control readouts were evaluated. A rat needle-puncture IVDD model was used to assess the effects of local intradiscal ESME delivery.
RESULTS: ESMEs more effectively improved NPC viability, reduced apoptosis and senescence-associated phenotypes, and corrected catabolic matrix imbalance than NSMEs. These effects were accompanied by reduced oxidative/JNK-associated stress signaling, lower mitochondria-derived ROS, improved mitochondrial membrane potential and network integrity, and LC3/p62 changes consistent with improved mitochondrial quality-control homeostasis. In vivo, local ESME delivery attenuated disc-height loss, preserved T2-weighted MRI signal, improved histological degeneration scores and supported matrix retention.
CONCLUSION: Exercise preconditioning enhanced the protective activity of skeletal muscle exosomes. Locally delivered ESMEs attenuated IVDD-associated degenerative phenotypes, supporting further development of exercise-derived extracellular vesicles as a local, cell-free strategy for avascular disc tissues. Clinical translation will require larger-animal validation, biodistribution and safety studies, and identification of the key bioactive components.

item.title: Serum IL-33/sST2 is associated with polymyositis/dermatomyositis complicated with interstitial lung disease.
item.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To investigate serum levels of interleukin-33 (IL-33) and soluble ST2 (sST2) in patients with polymyositis/dermatomyositis (PM/DM), and analyze their correlation with clinical indicators.
METHODS: Serum IL-33, sST2, and neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) marker cell-free DNA (cfDNA) were measured in 60 PM/DM patients and 20 healthy controls. The correlations between these indicators and their relationships with clinical data were analyzed. IL-33 expression in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) was detected by Western blot, and its effect on NETs formation was observed via high-content live-cell imaging.
RESULTS: PM/DM patients showed significantly elevated serum IL-33, sST2, and cfDNA levels compared with controls (all p < 0.01). ELISA-detected serum IL-33 levels showed no significant difference between PM/DM patients with and without ILD, while Western blot analysis revealed significantly higher IL-33 protein expression in PBMCs from the ILD group than from the non-ILD group. Of note, IL-33 expression at the cellular (PBMCs) level, but not serum IL-33, was associated with ILD in PM/DM patients. sST2 levels were also higher in PM/DM patients with ILD. IL-33 induced NETs formation in neutrophils. IL-33 and sST2 levels positively correlated with cfDNA and lung CT scores in PM/DM-ILD patients. Multiple linear regression identified IL-33, sST2, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) as independent factors for cfDNA. ROC analysis showed that the combination of sST2, ESR, and CRP yielded an AUC of 0.911 for diagnosing ILD, which was superior to any single indicator.
CONCLUSION: Elevated IL-33 and sST2 in PM/DM correlate with inflammation, muscle injury, ILD, and NETs formation, suggesting the IL-33/ST2 pathway may contribute to PM/DM-ILD pathogenesis by promoting NETs formation. Key Points • Serum IL-33 and sST2 levels are significantly elevated in PM/DM patients, and correlate with inflammation, muscle injury, and disease activity. • IL-33 promotes NETs formation in neutrophils, and serum cfDNA positively correlates with IL-33 and sST2, suggesting the IL-33/ST2 axis may contribute to PM/DM-ILD pathogenesis through inducing NETs. • sST2 has discriminative value for ILD in PM/DM, and its combination with ESR and CRP improves diagnostic accuracy (AUC = 0.911), supporting its potential as a clinical biomarker panel.
